## 3. ACCEPTABLE ENVIRONMENTAL RANGES

The following ranges apply to all collection areas. These values are based on ASHRAE Class B guidelines and have been tailored to the specific needs of the museum's collection.

### 3.1 Temperature

| Location Type | Acceptable Range (°C) | Preferred Range (°C) | Seasonal Adjustment |
|----------------|----------------------|----------------------|---------------------|
| Permanent Storage | 18.0 – 22.0 | 19.0 – 21.0 | None |
| Exhibition Galleries | 18.0 – 24.0 | 19.0 – 22.0 | Winter: 19.0 – 21.0; Summer: 20.0 – 23.0 |
| Paper Conservation Lab | 18.5 – 21.5 | 19.0 – 20.5 | None |
| Objects Conservation Studio | 18.0 – 22.0 | 19.0 – 21.0 | None |
| Textile Storage Annex | 16.0 – 20.0 | 17.0 – 19.0 | None |

### 3.2 Relative Humidity

| Location Type | Acceptable Range (% RH) | Preferred Range (% RH) | Maximum 24-hr Fluctuation |
|----------------|-------------------------|------------------------|---------------------------|
| Permanent Storage | 40 – 60 | 45 – 55 | ±5% |
| Exhibition Galleries | 40 – 60 | 45 – 55 | ±5% |
| Paper Conservation Lab | 45 – 55 | 48 – 52 | ±3% |
| Objects Conservation Studio | 40 – 55 | 45 – 50 | ±5% |
| Textile Storage Annex | 45 – 60 | 50 – 55 | ±5% |

### 3.3 Light

| Location Type | Maximum Illuminance (lux) | Maximum Annual Exposure (lux-hours) | UV Limit |
|----------------|---------------------------|-------------------------------------|----------|
| Permanent Storage (lights off when unoccupied) | 50 | 50,000 | 0 μW/lm |
| Exhibition Galleries – Light-Sensitive Materials | 50 | 50,000 | 10 μW/lm |
| Exhibition Galleries – Moderately Sensitive Materials | 150 | 300,000 | 10 μW/lm |
| Exhibition Galleries – Low Sensitivity Materials | 300 | 600,000 | 75 μW/lm |
| Conservation Laboratories | 300 | N/A (task lighting) | 75 μW/lm |
| Textile Storage Annex | 50 | 50,000 | 0 μW/lm |

**Note on Light Monitoring:** Lux readings are taken at object surface height, typically 1.5 meters above floor level for hanging works and at display case base height for 3-D objects. UV readings are taken at the same location as lux readings.
Sensor placement is critical to obtaining representative environmental data. The goal is to measure the conditions that collection objects actually experience, not the conditions in the center of a room or near HVAC supply vents. The following principles apply to all sensor installations:

### 4.2 Sensor Density Requirements

The number of sensors required for each space is determined by the size of the space, the sensitivity of the collection housed within it, and the stability of the environmental conditions. The following minimum densities apply:

| Space Type | Minimum Sensor Density | Notes |
|------------|------------------------|-------|
| Permanent Storage (small rooms < 50 m²) | 1 sensor per 25 m² | At least 2 sensors per room regardless of size |
| Permanent Storage (large rooms ≥ 50 m²) | 1 sensor per 50 m² | Additional sensors near exterior walls, doors, and known problem areas |
| Exhibition Galleries | 1 sensor per 100 m² | At least 1 sensor per gallery; additional sensors in cases and near light-sensitive displays |
| Paper Conservation Lab | 2 sensors (minimum) | One at bench height, one at storage/archival shelving height |
| Objects Conservation Studio | 2 sensors (minimum) | One at bench height, one near solvent/chemical storage area |
| Textile Storage Annex | 1 sensor per 40 m² | At least 3 sensors; placement must account for rolling racks and compact shelving |
| Display Cases | 1 sensor per case | Required for cases containing light-sensitive or hygroscopic materials |

### 4.3 Standard Mounting Heights

Sensors are mounted at the following heights depending on the space type:

| Space Type | Mounting Height | Notes |
|------------|-----------------|-------|
| Permanent Storage | 1.5 m | At object mid-height for standard shelving |
| Exhibition Galleries | 1.5 m | At object surface height for hanging works |
| Paper Conservation Lab | 1.2 m (bench) / 1.8 m (shelving) | Bench sensor monitors work surface conditions |
| Objects Conservation Studio | 1.2 m (bench) | Additional sensor at floor level if solvent storage is present |
| Textile Storage Annex | 1.5 m | On aisle ends, not on rolling racks |
| Display Cases | Interior center, at object height | Sensor must not touch object or case walls |

### 4.4 Display Case Monitoring

Display cases present a unique microclimate that may differ significantly from the surrounding gallery conditions. The following guidelines apply:

- Each display case containing light-sensitive materials (textiles, works on paper, photographs, watercolors) must have a dedicated temperature and RH sensor.
- Sensors are placed inside the case at object height, typically at the center of the display volume. The sensor must not be visible to visitors; position it behind a baffle or in a corner where it does not interfere with the display.
- The sensor cable should exit through a sealed port. Any opening must be gasketed to maintain the case's environmental integrity.
- Lux sensors for case interiors are placed at the same location as the temperature/RH sensor whenever possible. If a separate lux sensor is required, it is placed at the display surface plane, facing upward toward the light source.
- Case interior conditions are logged separately from gallery conditions. Data from case sensors is reviewed monthly to identify any drift or unexpected microclimate development.

## 5. Calibration Schedule and Procedures

### 5.1 Calibration Frequency

All environmental monitoring equipment is calibrated on a regular schedule. The frequency of calibration depends on the type of instrument and its criticality to collection care:
## 5. Calibration Schedule and Procedures (continued)

### 5.2 Calibration Intervals by Instrument Type

The following table lists the standard calibration intervals for each instrument category. Intervals are measured from the date of the most recent calibration, not from the date of purchase or installation. If an instrument fails a calibration check, it is removed from service immediately and the interval clock for its replacement begins on the date the replacement is first placed into active monitoring.

| Instrument Type | Calibration Interval | Calibration Method | Responsible Party |
|-----------------|----------------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Temperature/RH data loggers (gallery and storage) | 12 months | Two-point comparison against NIST-traceable reference at 20 °C / 50% RH and 25 °C / 60% RH | Facilities Department |
| Temperature/RH data loggers (display case interior) | 6 months | Same as above; performed in situ where possible | Conservation Department with Facilities support |
| Lux meters (handheld) | 12 months | Comparison against reference photometer at 50, 200, and 500 lux | Facilities Department |
| Lux sensors (fixed, in galleries or cases) | 12 months | In situ comparison against calibrated handheld meter | Conservation Department |
| Reference hygrometer (used for spot checks) | 6 months | Salt-solution verification at 33% and 75% RH | Facilities Department |
| Data logger software / clock synchronization | Quarterly | Verify timestamp accuracy against network time; adjust if drift exceeds ±2 minutes | Facilities Department |

Note: Any instrument that has been dropped, exposed to water, or subjected to a temperature excursion outside its rated operating range must be removed from service and recalibrated prior to further use, regardless of the scheduled interval.

### 5.3 Calibration Procedure

1. Prior to calibration, the instrument is inspected for physical damage, battery condition, and firmware version. Any issues are noted on the calibration worksheet (Form ENV-04).
2. The instrument is placed in a stable environment and allowed to equilibrate for a minimum of 60 minutes before readings are compared.
3. For temperature/RH loggers, readings are recorded at two points as specified in Section 5.2. The reference instrument and the unit under test are logged simultaneously at one-minute intervals for 15 minutes. The average difference is calculated.
4. Acceptance criteria:
   - Temperature: ±0.5 °C of reference
   - Relative humidity: ±3% RH of reference
   - Lux: ±5% of reference reading
5. If the instrument passes, the calibration date is updated in the Environmental Monitoring System (EMS) and a calibration label is affixed to the instrument body.
6. If the instrument fails, it is tagged "needs calibration" in the EMS and removed from service. A replacement unit is assigned from the spare inventory (see Section 5.5). The failed unit is sent for factory repair or replacement.
7. Calibration records are retained for a minimum of five years. Records include the instrument ID, calibration date, reference instrument ID, raw comparison data, and the name of the technician performing the calibration.

### 6. Alarm Thresholds and Response Procedures

Alarm thresholds are set to provide early warning of conditions that could damage collections. The values in Table 6.1 are the default thresholds for all monitored spaces. These values are reviewed annually during the November environmental review meeting and may be adjusted for specific galleries, cases, or storage areas when a collections risk assessment or a loan agreement requires tighter control.

| Parameter | Low Alarm | High Alarm | Critical Low | Critical High |
|-----------|-----------|------------|--------------|---------------|
| Temperature | 18.0 °C | 24.0 °C | 15.0 °C | 27.0 °C |
| Relative Humidity | 40% RH | 60% RH | 30% RH | 65% RH |
| Light (galleries, max hourly) | — | 200 lux | — | 300 lux |
| Light (textiles, max hourly) | — | 50 lux | — | 80 lux |
| UV (galleries) | — | 75 µW/lm | — | 100 µW/lm |

Alarms are generated by the Environmental Monitoring System (EMS) when a reading falls outside the configured range. The EMS logs the alarm event, the affected sensor, the value at the time of the alarm, and the duration of the excursion. Alarm events are retained in the EMS for five years.

#### 6.1 Alarm Tiers

Alarm events are classified into three tiers based on the severity and duration of the excursion.

- **Tier 1 (Advisory):** A single reading outside the normal range that returns to within range within one hour. No immediate action is required beyond acknowledging the alarm in the EMS. Advisory alarms are reviewed weekly by the Conservation Department.
- **Tier 2 (Action):** A reading outside the normal range that persists for more than one hour, or any reading outside the critical range. The Conservation duty officer is notified by text and email. The duty officer is responsible for investigating the cause and initiating corrective action.
- **Tier 3 (Emergency):** A reading outside the critical range that persists for more than 30 minutes, or any alarm indicating a possible equipment failure (e.g., sensor communication loss, HVAC fault). The Facilities Department is notified immediately, and the Conservation Department is engaged to assess potential collection impact.

#### 6.2 Response Responsibilities

| Tier | Primary Responder | Secondary Responder | Response Time |
|------|-------------------|---------------------|---------------|
| Tier 1 | Conservation staff on shift | — | Within 8 working hours |
| Tier 2 | Conservation duty officer | Facilities technician | Within 1 working hour |
| Tier 3 | Facilities Department | Conservation Department head | Immediate |

All alarm responses are documented in the EMS, including the cause of the excursion, the action taken, and the time the space returned to within acceptable limits. The response log is reviewed at the monthly joint Facilities/Conservation meeting.

#### 6.3 Common Causes of Alarm Events

The following conditions are the most frequently observed causes of alarm events in this facility. This list is not exhaustive; any unusual pattern should be reported to the Facilities Department.

- HVAC setpoint changes or scheduled maintenance that temporarily disables climate control.
- Exhibit case doors left open during installation or maintenance activity.
- Humidifier or dehumidifier water supply interruption.
- Seasonal transitions, particularly the onset of heating season in late October and the onset of cooling season in late April.
- Localized heat sources such as video projectors, track lighting, or people flow in small galleries.
- Sensor drift or sensor placement issues, particularly for loggers mounted too close to supply air diffusers or exterior walls.

Monitoring is continuous, 24 hours per day, 365 days per year. Data logging intervals are set to one hour for all environmental data loggers unless otherwise specified in this document. Manual spot checks are performed twice daily on weekdays during normal business hours (9:00 AM to 5:00 PM) and once on weekends by the security desk.

---

## 2. RESPONSIBILITIES

**Environmental Monitoring Specialist (Primary):** Sofia Reyes (Employee ID EMP00412) is the designated Environmental Monitoring Specialist. Sofia Reyes monitors all three sites: the main museum building, the off-site textile storage annex, and the conservation laboratories. This responsibility includes oversight of data collection, equipment maintenance, alarm response, and reporting.

**Facilities Manager:** Marcus Chen (Employee ID EMP00218) oversees the HVAC systems and coordinates with external contractors for repairs and scheduled maintenance.

**Head of Conservation:** Dr. Patricia Voss (Employee ID EMP00105) reviews monthly environmental reports and authorizes any changes to set points or alarm thresholds.

**Conservation Staff:** All conservation staff members are responsible for reporting any observed environmental anomalies to the Environmental Monitoring Specialist immediately. This includes unusual odors, visible condensation, sudden temperature changes, or apparent light damage.

**Security Personnel:** The security desk performs weekend spot checks and responds to environmental alarms outside of normal business hours.

## 3. ACCEPTABLE ENVIRONMENTAL RANGES

The following ranges apply to all collection areas. These values are based on ASHRAE Class B guidelines and have been tailored to the specific needs of the museum's collection.

### 3.1 Temperature

| Location Type | Acceptable Range (°C) | Preferred Range (°C) | Seasonal Adjustment |
|----------------|----------------------|----------------------|---------------------|

### 4.4 Display Case Monitoring

Display cases present a unique microclimate that may differ significantly from the surrounding gallery conditions. The following guidelines apply:

- Each display case containing light-sensitive materials (textiles, works on paper, photographs, watercolors) must have a dedicated temperature and RH sensor.
- Sensors are placed inside the case at object height, typically at the center of the display volume. The sensor must not be visible to visitors; position it behind a baffle or in a corner where it does not interfere with the display.
- The sensor cable should exit through a sealed port. Any opening must be gasketed to maintain the case's environmental integrity.
- Lux sensors for case interiors are placed at the same location as the temperature/RH sensor whenever possible. If a separate lux sensor is required, it is placed at the display surface plane, facing upward toward the light source.
- Case interior conditions are logged separately from gallery conditions. Data from case sensors is reviewed monthly to identify any drift or unexpected microclimate development.

### 5.2 Calibration Intervals by Instrument Type

The following table lists the standard calibration intervals for each instrument category. Intervals are measured from the date of the most recent calibration, not from the date of purchase or installation. If an instrument fails a calibration check, it is removed from service immediately and the interval clock for its replacement begins on the date the replacement is first placed into active monitoring.

| Instrument Type | Calibration Interval | Calibration Method | Responsible Party |
|-----------------|----------------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Temperature/RH data loggers (gallery and storage) | 12 months | Two-point comparison against NIST-traceable reference at 20 °C / 50% RH and 25 °C / 60% RH | Facilities Department |
| Temperature/RH data loggers (display case interior) | 6 months | Same as above; performed in situ where possible | Conservation Department with Facilities support |
| Lux meters (handheld) | 12 months | Comparison against reference photometer at 50, 200, and 500 lux | Facilities Department |
| Lux sensors (fixed, in galleries or cases) | 12 months | In situ comparison against calibrated handheld meter | Conservation Department |
| Reference hygrometer (used for spot checks) | 6 months | Salt-solution verification at 33% and 75% RH | Facilities Department |
| Data logger software / clock synchronization | Quarterly | Verify timestamp accuracy against network time; adjust if drift exceeds ±2 minutes | Facilities Department |

Note: Any instrument that has been dropped, exposed to water, or subjected to a temperature excursion outside its rated operating range must be removed from service and recalibrated prior to further use, regardless of the scheduled interval.

### 5.3 Calibration Procedure

1. Prior to calibration, the instrument is inspected for physical damage, battery condition, and firmware version. Any issues are noted on the calibration worksheet (Form ENV-04).
2. The instrument is placed in a stable environment and allowed to equilibrate for a minimum of 60 minutes before readings are compared.
3. For temperature/RH loggers, readings are recorded at two points as specified in Section 5.2. The reference instrument and the unit under test are logged simultaneously at one-minute intervals for 15 minutes. The average difference is calculated.
4. Acceptance criteria:
   - Temperature: ±0.5 °C of reference
   - Relative humidity: ±3% RH of reference
   - Lux: ±5% of reference reading
5. If the instrument passes, the calibration date is updated in the Environmental Monitoring System (EMS) and a calibration label is affixed to the instrument body.
6. If the instrument fails, it is tagged "needs calibration" in the EMS and removed from service. A replacement unit is assigned from the spare inventory (see Section 5.5). The failed unit is sent for factory repair or replacement.
7. Calibration records are retained for a minimum of five years. Records include the instrument ID, calibration date, reference instrument ID, raw comparison data, and the name of the technician performing the calibration.

### 6. Alarm Thresholds and Response Procedures

Alarm thresholds are set to provide early warning of conditions that could damage collections. The values in Table 6.1 are the default thresholds for all monitored spaces. These values are reviewed annually during the November environmental review meeting and may be adjusted for specific galleries, cases, or storage areas when a collections risk assessment or a loan agreement requires tighter control.

| Parameter | Low Alarm | High Alarm | Critical Low | Critical High |
|-----------|-----------|------------|--------------|---------------|
| Temperature | 18.0 °C | 24.0 °C | 15.0 °C | 27.0 °C |
| Relative Humidity | 40% RH | 60% RH | 30% RH | 65% RH |
| Light (galleries, max hourly) | — | 200 lux | — | 300 lux |
| Light (textiles, max hourly) | — | 50 lux | — | 80 lux |
| UV (galleries) | — | 75 µW/lm | — | 100 µW/lm |

Alarms are generated by the Environmental Monitoring System (EMS) when a reading falls outside the configured range. The EMS logs the alarm event, the affected sensor, the value at the time of the alarm, and the duration of the excursion. Alarm events are retained in the EMS for five years.

#### 6.1 Alarm Tiers

Alarm events are classified into three tiers based on the severity and duration of the excursion.

- **Tier 1 (Advisory):** A single reading outside the normal range that returns to within range within one hour. No immediate action is required beyond acknowledging the alarm in the EMS. Advisory alarms are reviewed weekly by the Conservation Department.
- **Tier 2 (Action):** A reading outside the normal range that persists for more than one hour, or any reading outside the critical range. The Conservation duty officer is notified by text and email. The duty officer is responsible for investigating the cause and initiating corrective action.
- **Tier 3 (Emergency):** A reading outside the critical range that persists for more than 30 minutes, or any alarm indicating a possible equipment failure (e.g., sensor communication loss, HVAC fault). The Facilities Department is notified immediately, and the Conservation Department is engaged to assess potential collection impact.

#### 6.2 Response Responsibilities

| Tier | Primary Responder | Secondary Responder | Response Time |
|------|-------------------|---------------------|---------------|
| Tier 1 | Conservation staff on shift | — | Within 8 working hours |
| Tier 2 | Conservation duty officer | Facilities technician | Within 1 working hour |
| Tier 3 | Facilities Department | Conservation Department head | Immediate |

All alarm responses are documented in the EMS, including the cause of the excursion, the action taken, and the time the space returned to within acceptable limits. The response log is reviewed at the monthly joint Facilities/Conservation meeting.

#### 6.3 Common Causes of Alarm Events

The following conditions are the most frequently observed causes of alarm events in this facility. This list is not exhaustive; any unusual pattern should be reported to the Facilities Department.

- HVAC setpoint changes or scheduled maintenance that temporarily disables climate control.
- Exhibit case doors left open during installation or maintenance activity.
- Humidifier or dehumidifier water supply interruption.
- Seasonal transitions, particularly the onset of heating season in late October and the onset of cooling season in late April.
- Localized heat sources such as video projectors, track lighting, or people flow in small galleries.
- Sensor drift or sensor placement issues, particularly for loggers mounted too close to supply air diffusers or exterior walls.
